doc.title: Pete Candoli interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 15, 1999

title: Metronome all-star date and replacing Cootie Williams with Benny Goodman
summary: Pete recalls an all-star date with Dorsey and Harry Edison, then six weeks with Goodman at the New Yorker Hotel, where musicians talked stocks.

story.theme_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the leader and his bands
story.community_name: Working for Benny Goodman: the perfectionist bandleader

blocks.x: So how did — did you eventually decide, let’s see, late 40s, early 50s, that the road thing was getting a little old?

No it wasn’t getting too old, not really. But I was into, I remember like in ’43 I think it was Tommy Dorsey’s band or ’42 or sometime, I took Ziggy’s place and I remember playing lead on an all-star Metronome date. And Sweets was there, Sweets, Harry Edison, my dear friend. We do a lot of the Blue Note things with Lionel Hampton and the Golden Men of Music, you know that. And I found an old album, and I don’t have any albums, this must have been really in storage. Tommy Dorsey was playing lead trombone, I was playing lead trumpet on the date, and there was four or five trumpet players. Sweets I remember being one of them. Dud Bascomb was another.

And I remember taking Cootie Williams’ place with Benny Goodman at the New Yorker Hotel. I was there I think for six weeks, and Vido Musso was on the band, Hymie Schertzer was playing lead, Brad McGowan on valve trombone. It was really a good band. But I didn’t care about anything. I had heard about “the ray” and things like that, how he used to think. But I remember the night before we opened up, Guy Lombardo’s band was there, and I was kind of snickering a little bit because it was Muzak compared to where I was looking. But it was great for what it was. I remember going in the back room and these guys that were with Benny they come in, oh hi, hi, and some were playing cards in the band room, and some were saying, “I think you ought to pick up a hundred shares of that AT&T and things like that. They were into that, as I was a kid. You understand? But to me it didn’t mean anything, because I had no idea what they were doing. But later I recognized they were into stocks and so on. I only cared about the music.

So it was kind of funny later on when I realized what was happening that I didn’t know. It’s the old story about Mark Twain saying I remember when I was 15 or 16 I remember my father just -- I was about 20, about four or five years later, I was amazed to learn how much he, my father, had learned. I was amazed how much I had learned, thinking back, what was really happening in reality.
That whole experience thing again, there you go.
